review:
Wargame: Red Dragon, despite its bare-bones naval combat, is the greatest Wargame to date. It is difficult to write a review in a traditional manner with this game as it has depth akin to a black hole, so I'm just going to list down in-depth pro-cons of this fantastic, fun game.

~PROS:

1. - [b] This game is [I] far [/I] more accessible than most folks give it credit to. [/b] The controls are not convoluted, nor do things have unnecessary functionalities or five thousand menus to grind through to complete simple tasks. This game is complex in the best possible way for a game of its caliber; the depth of its combat.
This strength makes the game an extremely enjoyable experience as none of it is bogged down by simulation-esque frivolities. Mechanically it is somewhat similar to games like StarCraft (this isn't [i] Harpoon [/i] or [i] Jane's Fleet Command [/i]), although the scale is increased one-hundred fold. The game is complicated only in that it requires not only knowledge of units and their roles, but also quick-thinking and problem solving. The learning curve is steep but I'll be damned if I didn't say I had a blast getting to the point where I could consistently win matches.

2. - [b] This is any political/military nut's dream. [/b] There is a reason why much of its consistent playerbase is made up of people from /pol/ (don't let that intimidate you, the community is leagues better than most skill-based RTSs). You can simulate any "What If" scenario using countries like the People's Republic of China and North Korea all the way down to nations such as Norway and Sweden. And the game's compelling campaign missions simulate this also; what if the U.K. had not peacefully given back Hong Kong, and had to defend against waves of PLA tanks? You can do everything from sending Navy SEALs behind enemy lines to destroy Soviet command structures to launching massive armored offensives using the latest modern equipment. And it is all (mostly) pinpoint accurate.

3. - [b] The game is well-built, diverse and reliable. [/b] They aren't kidding when they say [I] "1,450 units that have been meticulously reproduced from their source!" [/I] There are maps ranging from suburban sprawls to massive tracts of forest prime for special forces operations, using anything from Polish commandos to Czechoslovakian airborne. If you find the game enjoyable it is difficult to get away from, as there is so much content to explore and master. Every unit has an easy reference-sheet that you can view at any time, and all of them (save for PACT/NATO copies of Soviet/American equipment) have unique stats. Some countries have more options than others, but that is only to maintain realistic integrity. You cannot expect Norway to have a better military than the United States, but that doesn't mean they wont have superior niche units such as special forces. Countries like Poland and Czechoslovakia recently were balanced in a patch, making them up to snuff with everyone, so you can likely expect more free DLC patches to the other nations as well. Not only that, but this game is incredibly resistant to technical issues. I have not crashed once in all my hours of playing (this always varies with different machines, though, but I've but this game through hell and its always been fine). Your experience will rarely be interrupted.

4. - [b] Deckbuilding is EXTREMELY enjoyable. [/b] I've spent half of the time in this game making decks. It may just be personal preference, but because of the thousand+ units, you can find yourself sinking a lot of time into this; not out of necessity, but simply to create fun and personalized armies.

Those are my major PROs. Now I believe I should address the hindrances to the gameplay here.

~CONS:

1. - [b] Naval combat is easily the weakest part of the game. [/b] It is painful saying that, honestly, but that is the truth. It is horribly imbalanced, inaccurate and barebones compared to every other part of the game, and this is especially true in NATO's case, but I'll get to that later.
Combat revolves around three principles which usually do not interact with eachother whatsoever; you either mass missile-heavy ships and launch them all at the same time at another blob of ships hoping to get through its CIWS guns, mass low-cost ships and rush them at lower numbers of expensive ships to stun them with cannonfire, or mass aircraft and do the same thing mentioned with the first option. It makes for a very uninspired and boring experience, and although it [I] somewhat [/I] resembles small-unit naval combat well, beyond that it is entirely inaccurate. There are no submarines, nor aircraft carriers, no exciting fringe ships such as Soviet battleships. You get a very thin selection of classes which makes large engagements very stale.
The worst part of this feature is that it is terribly imbalanced in favor of PACT. Most of NATO's ships are comprised of Japanese ships, with occasional exceptions. The flagship of NATO is some ship I've never heard of called a "Kongo." No Ticonderoga or Arleigh Burke's here, folks. Just awful surface ships with inaccurately-modeled weapons (harpoons can't hit anything!). This is in vast contrast to Soviet ships which outclass them in nearly every category; superior accuracy, firepower, durability, range, etc. Their flagships are the popular Udaloy/Sovremenny class destroyers, which are infinitely more famous than the Kongo.
Riverboats can be fun (the napalm Minotaur can torch vast swatches of riverland in fire, the SHMEL can launch hundreds of missiles) but are ultimately uninspired as they, too, revolve around massing and throwing at the enemy.

2. - [b] Frustration comes easy at times. [/b] Games drag on, especially if you're losing. Comebacks happen often but many times the case comes down to you being dominated for half an hour, and it makes this game a huge time sinkhole. You learn slowly and losses can be draining once you feel you've gotten better at the game than before; it takes constitution to get to a point where the shoe is on the other foot. It is difficult to be carried in this game as well, since it usually comes down to whatever team is best coordinated wins. This is not always the case, as skill is definitely involved and one person on a team can slaughter half the enemy's army through shrewd positioning, but that's an "If."


~PERSONAL RECOMMENDATION:
[b] Yes. [/b] If you have an interest in modern military combat, or even if you just like a fun and deep RTS, this is the game for you. I adore it for all of the reasons above, and I think the pros vastly outweigh the cons with this gem of a title. If you can spare the cash and you like the concept, go for it. You won't be disappointed.

800+ hours in Wargame Red Dragon
hundreds of hours on previous wargames.

This is one of the best, if not the best real time strategy ever made.

Wargame has many realistic features such as: ammo, gasoline, morale, veterancy, supplies, recon, with countless possibilities and methods of securing victory, which fit nicely making this a realistic game, while not too complicated.

The game has a steep learning curve, but if you want to play the best RTS out there, you have to get this game!

PS: The devs care about the community and suggested changes are sometimes implemented, especially if it benefits the gameplay, or balance, while staying as close to realism as possible.

I'm surprised that I still haven't written a review of this game yet.

It's a great game; in my opinion the most polished Wargame of the series. Although European Escalation has the superior campaign. Scripted campaigns (European Escalation) are a lot more fun to play than a sandbox-y campaign where you play against an extremely predictable AI on rezoned multiplayer maps (AirLand Battle and Red Dragon).

Wargame's always been an RTS with greater focus on force composition and positioning rather than micromanagement. Deathballing that you typically see in Starcraft/Command and Conquer does not work here. Your forces have to be spread out, ready to support eachother, and be able to take their objectives on the map.

The force you deploy in multiplayer is your "deck", which you build not unlike decks in popular card games such as Hearthstone. Select an alliance/coalition/nation, create a deck with logistics, infantry, support, aircraft, navy, tanks, and the like and deploy that deck in battle. Since the game uses a deck system, like the cards in a real life deck of cards you're limited in the number of units you can deploy. Try not to lose both your Su-27PU's in one go.

The game also places emphasis on logistics, which I have never before seen in an RTS game. All units have health, fuel value, and ammo value for EVERY weapon (including coaxial machine guns). You must sustain your forces through a well maintained logistics line. Supplies are also limited (and the amount of supply you have depends on how much supply units you've included in your deck) so use sparingly.

Combat is fairly realistic. Engagement ranges seem more plausible than in traditional RTS games (where a marine can only see and fire up to 10 feet in front of him).

The game is extremely well optimized; I was able to run it at a steady 40-60 FPS on a laptop that could only use Intel integrated graphics (albiet on medium settings). You can zoom all the way out so that you can see the entire map and your units icons, or zoom all the way in to see combat from a footman's perspective.

The naval portion is a bit gimmicky. Sure, sometimes it's fun to play with ships but the combat is not nearly as exciting or engaging as land/air combat. However, amphibious land units does open up more tactical options since you're not 100% restricted to crossing bridges or chokepoints.

As a Cold War history buff, having access to over 1400+ real life units from over a multitude of countries spanning North America, Europe, and Asia is extremely exciting as well. Even now I'm still overwhelmed at how many variants of Abrams tanks there are (M1 Abrams, M1IP Abrams, M1A1 Abrams, M1A1HA Abrams, M1A1HC Abrams, M1A2 Abrams).

I don't play this game as much nowadays, but only because I've played it almost exclusively for the past few years and it feels slightly stale to me now (although I do get on every now and then). Wargame: Red Dragon is one of the few games I've bought that has kept me entertained for so long.

A warning: this game is not meant for everyone.

So, Wargame is 75% off and you're here in the reviews trying to figure out whether to buy it or not. Well if you like a (mostly) realistic strategy game then Wargame is for you. But beware of the steep learning curve ahead. While there are some faults with this game such as semi incompetent AI and cheesy multiplayer starting strats the game is mostly good. With over 1500 real life units to choose from across a ton of countries and coalitions you have plenty of deck combinations to choose. I've played all 3 iterations of wargame and I can say that while they all have their pros and cons Wargame Red Dragon is the one to get. 

Check out the subreddit (/r/wargame) for guides and communities for people to play with.

As I'm typing this, I have nearly 600 hours on this game and I'm finally almost sort of good at it.

Wargame is my first real RTS (Read: Not a 2D flash game) and in retrospect that may have been a terrible mistake, because this game will flat out annihilate you if you don't know what you're doing, which you probably won't because there's a LOT to know. In other words, if you're new to Wargame, expect to lose a few times.

The trailer was not joking when it said there were over oople-bajillion units in the game. Admittedly, a lot of them are similar or are reskins, but most of them have vastly different stats. For example, there's a cheap, baseline T-72 which is basically a hunk of garbage with tracks and a gun on it, that bursts into flames if the tank commander sneezes. Then there's the highly modernized T-72s that will rip other tanks apart from 2000 meters and shrug off rockets as it roars across the battlefield, powered by diesel, the screams of the innocent, and human souls. Now, you can easily check the stats of a unit in-game by pressing "i", but memorizing them to some extent is helpful. But that's not the point. The point is, if you don't know what you're up against, there's a good chance you're going to get absolutely destroyed.

Once you have a vague understanding of what each unit does sort of, you have to learn how to counter each type. It's kind of like rock paper scissors, except nothing completely beats anything and there's several ways to lose. For example, tank beats infantry unless the infantry are at short range or have an ATGM. Infantry beats anything at short range. Infantry that are good at killing other infantry, beat infantry. Artillery also beats infantry. Plane also beats infantry but not infantry with MANPADs. SAM beats plane, unless the SAM is radar and the plane is SEAD.  Plane beats SAM if the SAM is garbage but only if the plane is ground attack, in certain situations, maybe. Everything on the battlefield plays a different role and you have to find a way to make that role work for you in the grand scheme of things. Learning how to do that can be difficult.

Not only do you have to know what kills what and when and how, but you also need to know the gameplay mechanics too. For example, you need to understand how combat stress affects your units, and how to use that to your advantage by making your enemies scream and cry and soil themselves before you start actually seriously trying to kill them. You need to know how reconnaisance works so you can find your enemy in the first place so that you can actually kill them. You need to figure out how to resupply your units so they don't turn into 60 tonne paperweights, and how to keep your supply units safe so they don't turn into an expensive and tactically ineffective fireball.

Those are just basic gameplay mechanics too. That doesn't even scratch the surface of using tactics and mindgames to actually defeat your enemy.

Wargame will throw you for a loop. This is the only RTS I've really gotten into and my friends who I've suckered into playing it all agree that this is something else. It will take some time to get past the learning curve. No matter how many hours you sink into it, your tactics will keep changing, you'll keep trying different things, but you will never perfect your strategy because a perfect strategy does not exist. This game will challenge you to learn. It will challenge you to think. It will challenge you to adapt, and it will challenge you a lot. But once you start to overcome these challenges, it becomes extremely satisfying to finally win. To lay crushing defeat on your enemies. To know you came from knowing nothing to feeling like a master of warfare.

As I'm typing this, I have nearly 600 hours on this game and I'm finally almost sort of good at it.

Tommorrow, I'll probably play it again and be a little bit better.

I would definitely reccomend this game. Just know that the learning curve is kind of steep.

Got into the closed beta for my dedication to the series, and was not disappointed at all. China could use a little buff considering the fact that the game is called Red Dragon after all, and half of China's within time frame units have been questionably ommitted. Naval warfare could use a little tweaking as well, because its implementation was poor at first. However the upcoming naval patch notes look extremely promising.

In terms of improvement over the AirlandBattle, this game has done it all. Land battles are now far more realistic, intense, and tactical thanks to some of the revolutionary changes that Eugen has made in map design, pace, and terrain. Indeed, this game has taken the openness and unlimited tactical/strategic opportunities that were the trademark of W:EE, and combined them with the ferocity that was characteristic of W:AB battles.

But overall, from my many hours of closed beta testing, this is the ultimate culmination of the awesome Wargame series. The enormous scale, realistic terrain, and the unlimited tactical, operational and even strategic options that this glorious game provides has never ceased to amaze me. Indeed, this is any amateur wargamer's/armchair general's (like myself) wet dream, and I would fully recommend this to anyone seeking an immersive, immense, and ultimately fulfilling historical/military experience.

Outstanding quality RTS that any military nut would enjoy.  Will also stress out your grey matter, too.  If you aren't familiar with the Wargame series, it's a borderline strategic simulator more than an RTS. No base building, no real resources (besides point income from holding sectors), and every unit has morale, health, ammo, and fuel that needs to be tended to carefully with supply lines.  

The scale is unlike what most other games in the genre offer.  It reminds me almost of the original Supreme Commander in terms of sher volume of units on the field and map size.  Every unit you take into battle will never come back alive once destroyed, and you need to make your own decks of units to take into battle, which is almost a kind of game in itself...finding the right unit combos or roles to take.  One of the major reasons I recommend this game is because of that.

The army variety and unit selection is also awe inspiring.  You can pick from about 1,500 units, all modeled correctly to their real counterpart and act like the real one too.  Nations to build from include the US, Canada, France, UK, Germany, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Poland, Russia, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, China, and Best Korea (I mean North Korea).  There's an army for everyone's taste and they all feel and play unique.

Naval battles need some work and balancing, though, but it also may be just the nature of modern warfare on the ocean.  It revolves around who makes the biggest ship blob and has the best radar gattling gun screen to stop incomming cruise missiles.  

Overall if you wanna work your brain a little in an RTS and focus entirely on the war and not the bases/economy, this is the thing for you.

400h gametime and played this game since the start of 2016, I'm here to inform you of the pros and cons of this unique game and hopefully drag you in as I myself am in the opinion that every wannabe Tactician (not strategist, they're a different breed) should play this game.   ... except if the cons looks too bad and overshadows the pros.

Pros:
1) Unique Strategy game "gameplay" = Unlike most RTS Strategy games, Wargame isn't about gathering resources on a certain part in the map and building factories to spend said resources to pump out units. Instead, before you would go into a match, you'd need to create a "Deck" of unit cards... kinda like YuGiOh except with Real life Military units. Once on the battlefield, you are assigned points depending on the game settings of the host and spend those points to deploy your "Units" from the Deck that you've made. Deck making is somewhat complex and won't be mentioned here. So after you deployed your units, you'd maneuvre them around the map and beat up your opponent on the field. Keep in mind that you do earn income to purchase more units overtime and it increases depending on the gamemode, or not at all.

2) Nice Graphics and Unit models = The map designs are clean enough and looks good enough, typical of your average everyday modern Strategy Game... but the real charm lies in the details of the ingame units... for the creators have faithfully stuck with the real designs of units as they are real life, all down to that tiny little hook and hose you see on that tiny tiny tank, indeed it would be there too in real life! and there are about like 500 units in the game so...

3) Diverse units and tactical layer = There are around 500 units in this game, each with their own categories and uses. And the thing is, almost every unit has their uses, from the cheap Militia to the deadly Special Forces; the deadly T-72 with upgrades to the lowly T-55; Don't let the prices fool you, no one will buy the most-expensive thing because they aren't "Cost-efficient", so you'll pretty much see every unit in the game thrown at you or used by you by the time you hit 200h gametime.

4) Well-paced game flow = Wargame Red Dragon is a quick RTS, it ain't slow as there is not wait time to purchase and train units then a lag before it spawns out of the Barracks or some mumbo jumbo. Once you place your units, SCRAM! issue those orders, get them rolling, you want to be the FIRST to the battlefield (If possible) as Sun Tzu once said, but I forgot his full quote... goes something like reaching there by noon and digging in or some ching chong. Anyways, the units aren't slow and sluggish either as the game speeds them up compared to their real life counterpart. The idea is that the battlefield you're in is actually raging on for hours instead of the 40m the game timer is set to.

5) No Microtransactions = Thats a Pros right? folks these days like to make a fuss about em

Cons
1) No good tutorial offered by the game itself = The game offers no decent tutorial so you'd need to learn from either others, guides, videos. Maybe this could be a pros since it forces the person to adapt, get creative and formulate his or her own playstyle along the way after absorbing many lessons as there really isn't a "1 way to win all games" playstyle.

2) An odd community = From my own experience you will encounter lots of people who will either keep silent or cuss at you the minute before the game begins. It get's worse by a cube root in team games and then multiplied by pie once a team starts winning and the other starts losing as they taunt the loser and the loser taunts the "weakest" player in their own team. Rarely is there any chivalry in the community, 1v1s are silent commanders facing each other and team games are "I did well but my teammates squandered my efforts so I abuse them" You rarely make friends here... but, there have been a few exceptions.

3) A community that are frightened easily = In most multiplayer game lobbies, it takes 3x longer than usual to finally start, the issue for this is that people always leave. Why do they always leave? because they checked the stats of their opponents and go "Oh, he's 30 levels higher than me and has an 80% winrate, I'm gonna lose so I'm gonna f**k off." I see this attitude everyday, complaining about "stacked" teams. Sure, they may be stacked but they might be friends and just want to play together, and neither are they stopping you from bringing a stack of friends. And if you're afraid of losing, how do you expect to learn? what will you gain? will you only play "Easy" games with people that are low in level and horrid winrate? This attitude needs to stop and people should just play the game regardless of the statistics of their opponents. So what if you lose? Atleast you learned something, you're marginally better than your previous self before the game started. Be happy and never Stat-check and leave, Commanders in real-life don't check their opponents stats too ya know.

4) Random unit debuffs = I get that in real life, plans never survive contact with the enemy, but can you be blamed when you're launching an assault and for some reason your most-expensive tank or Anti-Air vehicle gets "Detracked" or "Stuck in Mud" ? ... This is a rather bad feature in my opinion and should be removed. 

5) A small proffesional army = By this I mean a small playerbase. The game is rather... old, but gold! Nonetheless, this game really does not appeal to many RTS Gamers except oddballs like me I suppose

6) The Navy = As in real life, the Navy cannot win wars by itself. They merely support campaigns. It gets worst for the typical Napoleonic-era Admiral as Battleships really become obsolete compared to the Aircraft Carrier. Now to win Navy, you'd either bring submarines (nonexistent in Wargame) or Aircraft Carriers (Also Nonexistent) and have an Airwar but with Frigates at the bottom shooting. That's pretty much what Naval battles are like. The ships also turn oddly if you were to issue an order to turn 180 degrees. Gunboats do have a part to play too when providing coastal Fire support. If you're looking for large naval clashes, don't bother because they too won't happen in real life.

Neutrals (Can be good or bad depending on the individual)

1) Steep Learning Curve = This game is hard and requires skills, knowledge, and luck. You will lose a lot. So this means if you're a casual gamer, you're gonna eat dirt a lot. This is bad as well, hard game, hard life for you but good in a sense that you'd be facing dedicated players who are in to win and of high quality (somewhat).

2) Cold War Era = This game takes place at the end of the cold war (1990-ish) and a clash of ideologies occur. Either pick Vodka, Champagne or Rum

3) If it is your cup of tea, then I hope you won't mind spending hours of your life on it.

4) Warchat = In the main menu of the game when you first enter, you can chat with players around the globe to the left. This chat is rather hard to describe. It's a mixture of everything imaginable if the North Pole and South Pole were squished and launched into another dimension. There is everything there from Geopolitics, Holocaust Remembrance, Stalinium Production Protocols and How Mao Zedong invented coconuts. But don't worry, if you do ask a serious game-related question, you're going to be given a serious answer (From the answerer's point of view anyways)

5) The Battlefield goes East = In the previous game, it was in Europe. In Red Dragon, it's mostly in Asia. I hope you enjoy generic Asian house designs.

I would have to classify Wargame as my favorite RTS of all time. Here is my rundown of the game.

You will like this game if you enjoy battles that depend upon knowledge, tactics, and force composition for victory. You will enjoy this game if you dont like base building or economy management in an rts and prefer to focus on gaining territory and destroying enemy units. You will enjoy this game if you like a mostly realistic approach to war, including logistical supply lines, reconnaisance, artillery, and aerial attack that are lacking or understated in most rts games.

You will not like this game if you feel base building and economy are essential to rts games. You will not like this game if you want a simple rts. You will not like this game if you like micromanagement of units and twitchy gameplay like in a starcraft game.

Now here are some need to know things. The game's tutorial sucks. Go watch some youtube tutorials and gameplay videos to learn better. 1-2 games watched should be enough to learn the basics of how to play. That leads into the second thing. Mastering this will take time, and the learning curve is steep for 2 reasons. Knowledge of the differences in the units in this game is critical to long term success, and identifying whether the T72 variant shooting at you is a 50 point cheap tank or a 150 point expensive tank is very important. This means that learning what all the different stats for each weapon type mean is important to know the capabilities of a given friendly or enemy unit, and then to know what capabilities of the hundreds of units in the game have based on that. This isnt extremely complicated, as there are several weapon types even if the individual weapons are different damage values, but it is time consuming to learn and memorize this.

 This is the steep learning curve mentioned in several reviews for this game. But what it does mean is that those who persevere through early losses as they familiarize themselves with the game are rewarded with a deep and satisfying strategy title that emphasizes combat itself and knowledge of the enemy to gain victory.

Now lets get to deck building. As there is no base building or economy to speak of in the game, you army is determined before you enter battle, when you build a deck. Every army has a certain amount of points it have total and every unit you put in the deck counts against that point total. It is important to look at unit composition and strategy at this point, but dont worry - even veteran wargame players routinely adjust their deck compositions for maximum effectiveness, and you should expect no less as a newbie. The deck builder is where you go to look at the stats for all the units and it really helps out with learning the game before and after a match to look up a unit that did well against you to see why it did well.

Last but not least, visit the eugen forums and also ask players in the chat for advice. There are trolls, true, but there are also people who will help out with any questions you have despite how stupidly childish and amusing the chat may seem (i enjoy just watching the chat sometimes, its really funny).


Overall, I give the game a 10/10 because I have never played an rts this much, or liked one this much, since command and conquer generals and the first starcraft. And now I cant go back to those because this is so much better.
This game would be better if there was mod support so people could create custom campaigns and factions.

Future classic. The quintessential Cold War game. Very active multiplayer (as of April 2019),  probably will be until servers stay up, due to its quality and uniqueness. 

Vast number of nations to pick from. Game lured me in with Yugoslavia DLC pack, which in itself is very unique. No other game that I know of lets you play as Yugoslavia. 

If casual multiplayer is your thing, the 10v10 servers are perfect for beginners. Being slower paced, they allow you to learn the ropes & have fun doing it. The 1v1 and 4v4 modes are more serious and fast paced akin to starcraft or other high octane RTS.

Servers are up 24/7. I never have to wait long to grab a lobby, and soon after the game starts. During prime time it's instant with many lobbies up. Bellow I'll include a write up on getting started in multiplayer.
Lots can be said about the community but it's definitely a cult niche, take a look at subreddit /r/wargame. Memes being put out on a weekly basis five years after game release says enough by itself. 

=======================================================================

Beginners intro to Multiplayer: 

10v10 are the noob friendly games, they remind of warcraft 3 customs. You control only portions of the whole army which allows you to focus on micro, and really grasp the mechanics. 10v10 Tacticals are very much suited for solo learning. They give you ample time to make your decisions and observe how others play. It's more like a moba with less units to control and you dont feel as overwhelmed. Once you get ahead of the game you can move on to faster modes that are more akin to traditional RTS if you so wish. 

In said tacticals pick your niche and learn it well. You can stick with your choice of specialty, say tanks. When you learn tanks in and out expand to another niche say infantry and eventually stick to one or be an all rounder. Myself i stick to air, but sometimes i learn different things due to boredom or wanting to win. During the game, focus on securing a sector and observe how others play, their spacing in particular and what units they take.

When you get enough of tactical you can move on to different modes that require faster decision making due to responsibility of sheer number of units. It becomes less of a micro/tactic game and more of a macro/strategic game. Use the knowledge you learned and you wont feel so overwhelmed. You can like myself just stay in tacticals if that's the game pacing you prefer. Beware of elitism here, there is no right way or wrong way to play this game so explore until you find the mode that suits you.

Also recommend picking a nation or coalition and sticking with it for some time so you can refine your deck (a "deck" is the units available to call up, which you can customize in the armory) . If you change a lot you might not learn what works in a deck and what doesn't. There is a lot to memorize but it's pretty much a joy to do if you take it easy.

And lastly, dont take heed to toxic comments during the game, plenty of hotheads around in cold war ;) Hope you find your game mode and stick around because this game has a lot to offer. Incredible scope & depth. 

Enjoy the Cold War & Have fun!

Ahh where to begin. Well, this certainly isn't your average RTS. Far from it in fact. This is frankly the kind of strategy game I've been hoping to see for over ten years. Now, I have heard some say that you really need to be a military or cold war history enthusiast in order to appreciate Wargame. I may be biased as I have studied military weapon systems since I was a little kid, but I have to disagree. From the standpoint of an RTS game, I believe it is unmatched and I will give some reasons why.

It’s actually a bit difficult to compare to other games... see with many RTS games you're building your base, having little skirmishes toward the beginning to gain unit experience, with the ultimate goal of massing units for a big push. With Wargame, there is no base building... it is all actual military maneuvers, weapon system knowledge, use of cover and concealment both for survivability and ambush, use of recon to spot enemy units for more combat oriented units, gaining Line of Sight (LOS) prior to and maintaining it during engagements (more difficult than it sounds), use of support systems such as Artillery, AAA, and SAMs to provide cover for advancing infantry and armored units, use of special forces infantry to wreak havoc behind enemy lines, capitalizing on terrain features to enable better LOS, spreading out of units so that a single airstrike won't eliminate half your assault force... but not so thin that they cannot cover each other. At the beginning of a match, there is usually a push to gain strategic positions (which supply reinforcement points) and dig in, then using recon to find gaps in enemy defenses and pushing through, encircling the enemy and/or simply cutting off their supply routes and territories. So... Wargame really is an interesting combination, it’s slow like a chess game at times... and then in a matter of literally seconds it can turn into a massive brawl.

In multi-player, which is really the heart of the game, it utilizes a "Deck" system where you will pick and choose what units you wish to deploy into battle not terribly dissimilar to the Total War series of games. Thinking of it like a deck of cards, each one can only field a certain number of units... and once they're gone... they're gone. More advanced or higher trained units will mean that you will only be able to field a very limited number of them, making highly specialized extremely advanced Decks very difficult to play with as EVERY unit loss is a major one... but if you are very careful, and very clever, you can win.

Bringing more units into battle requires reinforcement points, which are gained by capturing strategic points on the map. While this system will sound familiar, it plays out differently than in most RTS games in that not just any unit can capture and hold a point. In fact, a single insignificant and vulnerable command jeep or other "CP" unit can capture and hold a point. If the enemy discovers this command unit, then you are just one artillery or air strike away from losing the point and having to bring forward another CP unit to secure it again.

Another system worth mentioning is support via supply trucks and helicopters. Every unit can run out of ammunition, and any unit utilizing a combustion engine will run out of fuel. The only way to keep your units in the fight is to resupply them utilizing cargo transports. These supply units are very vulnerable... they have no defensive weapon systems, and little to no armor. Special Forces units can ambush and capture enemy supply units, so if your enemy is pounding you with a constant barrage of weapons fire... chances are there is a major resupply operation in progress and if you can disrupt that, you can deal a crippling blow to your adversary. With resupply made impossible, your opponent's constant spam of shells and bullets will render his units helplessly dry on ammunition... easy targets.

Air forces are a big part of the game. Frankly a single well executed air strike can shut down an entire assault, and force your opponent into a defensive posture... but that is not to say that attacks from the air are TOO powerful. In fact, aerial units are very easy to shoot down, very expensive, and fixed wing aircraft can only fly for a short period of time before they have to bug out due to low fuel. Jets can also be particularly difficult to utilize effectively because most of the time the enemy will cover their ground forces with AAA and SAM units. However, in the off chance your opponent miscalculates or sends his forces in with little to no cover... responding with a couple A-10 Warthogs along with fighter cover and witnessing the destruction they are capable of is truly mezmerizing.

Now, I haven't messed around so much with the naval aspect introduced in Red Dragon... but there are some balance issues and tweaking to be made there. However, for ground forces, the game is amazing, made even more so through the use of amphibious units. Your opponent think that you're helpless against his wall of tanks overlooking the lone bridge in the area? Not a problem, send in a group of amphibious tanks or anti-tank missile equipped vehicles to traverse the river around the flank and put fire into the sides of the aforementioned problem. Did I mention that all vehicles, armor, helicopters have differing top, front, back, and side armor levels? Tank armor is usually very strong to the front, and weaker in the rear or side... makes flanking maneuvers or ambushes on unsuspecting armored units quite devastating.

In closing, the learning curve is high, the 1300 units is daunting to think about, and the pacing may not be what everyone is looking for. It can be very slow and almost chess-like at times, and then turn into a firefight with unrivaled intensity. If you're looking for a unique blend of game and simulation, that you could play for years and still learn new things, it's tough to beat Wargame.

I absolutely love this game. I have a blast doing what I do. The only downsides and issues I personally have with the game (and this might even be positives for some players) is that this game can be very micro-manage heavy. Steel Division 2 has spoiled me with its unit autonomy features and gimmicks, and since playing that game, the micro-managing aspect of this game has become even more of a downer for me. To be fair though, a ton of rts games now are a bit annoying with all the micro-managing that has to be done. I am supposed to be managing a massive fighting force that is literally countless platoons and even a few battalions in size. I shouldn't have to worry about pretty basic stuff that should be decided and done at literally the squad/vehicle crew level. If one of my tanks engages the enemy at his 9 o'clock, he should turn and face the tank at his 9 o'clock. Now I get that doesn't work as cleanly when you are being attacked from multiple directions, but I'd assume the tank should prioritize which direction the most dangerous incoming fire is coming from and face that direction. At this point though I am more or less just complaining about lots of different rts games, not just Wargame: Red Dragon. I also assume that the computing power and resources needed to program the ai to be that effective is quite large when you having dozens of tanks and other units on the field interacting with one another. Okay, I'm getting off topic here so lets bring it back to the game review.

Unit fuel, or "autonomy" as it is called in game, is another feature that kinda seems like a downer to me, or at least the way they implemented it into the game. Unit autonomy is a stat that is present on all ground and air vehicles in game, and is pretty much just another name for how much the gas tank can hold in each unit. Yes, fuel is a factor you have to consider when playing this game. For some that's a big turn off, for others, a cool and realistic feature. It might very well be if the stat was reflective or at least somewhat representative of the vehicles' actual fuel capacity and mileage in real life. For every ground unit it feels way too small and just an artificial constraint made to help balance units out. For helicopters it can feel the same as well. If a unit runs out of fuel, you have to risk bringing up a supply vehicle to refuel it, or it will just sit wherever it ran out of fuel at. That part I am fine with. What I don't like is what I stated previously, the fuel tanks simply aren't big enough or anywhere near their real life counterparts. The map sizes and combat ranges are definitely much larger in this game than in many other rts games, but still not really big enough in my opinion to warrant having to worry about fuel, at least at the level it currently does. Planes are the only exception to this rule, and that is simply so that they don't just loiter 500 feet above the battlefield the entire match above each player's starting zone, flying in a tight circle non-stop. Some planes present in game probably could in real life but for the sake of immersion they don't. Most planes can stay well longer than they need to drop their ordinance and get outta there. For planes, that's fine with me. For all the other units, not so much. You have to refuel your units multiple times during a match, which can be anywhere between 20 minutes to an hour or more. At most you should only have to do that maybe once in that time frame, twice if you are really playing a super long game. I'd prefer it if they treated fuel like they do in Steel Division 2, something that only affects air units. (To be honest, Steel Division 2's units and map sizes are where refueling would actually be much more appropriate if you are going by their real life counterparts, as tanks in the second world war got fuel mileage which was just about what you imaged it would be, awful.) I assume that they didn't include a stat for ground vehicle fuel for the sake of gameplay, which is alright to me. I wish they would retroactively just update this game and let the only logistical needs you have to worry about be health and ammo.

One thing that doesn't really affect how I would rate the game but would definitely love is official mod support. I really believe this game would absolutely spike in popularity and have much more longevity than it does now (which is already impressive but that may be because there isn't a game like it, or at least doesn't do what it does nearly as well) if players could finally be able to make their own maps, and adjust unit characteristics, attributes, and skins without having to mess with this game's very... weird and odd coding.

Obviously, this is all just my opinion, and it may sound like I was just going on about the negatives of this game, but I'd argue the positives far outweigh the negatives. There really isn't a game like this that takes place in a modern setting and at this scale. It isn't a masterpiece, but it definitely is a work of art. It's not for everyone, but I definitely feel that a lot of people that this game is for doesn't even know this game exists. I'd argue it is worth about $29.99, and if it ever goes on sale for $19.99 or less, then it is a steal.

One last thing, then I'll quit: the community in this game is extremely toxic, like on another level sometimes. If you are easily offended by people, I'd recommend you either turn the in game chat off or not play at all. Trolling and racism is very prevalent in the in game chat. It is so prevalent that it's almost meme-like. Most of the people are probably trolling, but it is possible that some of them do mean what they say, which can be very homophobic/racist/anti-semitic/etc. and there is no chat moderation as far as I am aware. It doesn't really bother me because I think most of them are probably trolling. Obviously that doesn't make what they say okay or alright by any means, but it is what it is. All you can do is add those people to your ignore list and move on. It can be so absurd at times you can't help but laugh. Not everyone will have the same reaction as me though, so if you are easily offended, just turn off/mute the in game chat.

This review may not please the multiplayer only/PvP players in the crowd but I thought I would write up a review from the perspective of someone who mostly only plays single player (campaign, skirmish) or co-op with friends against the AI. This review is in no way implying that single player is somehow more important than anything else objectively, just that it is personally one of my primary concerns.

  With that disclaimer out of the way, let's get down to it. 

  Wargame: Red Dragon is probably the worst iteration of the series when it comes to single player. All the major elements like a vast selection of units and interesting maps are there but the AI is not just bad, it is pretty much the worst AI I have ever seen. For example, if you give the AI a deck with a single selection of T-55's, a single selection of BMP's, and perhaps a single selection of Mi-8's, they will first send every T-55, then when you blow them up, they will rush you with BMP's, when you blow them all up, they will send Mi-8's. There is not a whole lot of actual tactics or nuance on display (even when compared to the AI of prior Wargame titles) and the single player just becomes boring at best and annoying at worst. 

  The other issue for single player/co-op types is the perhaps over-zealous amount of deck balancing that has happend since the game first came out. While I am sure all the different unit "cards" are very balanced and make for solid competitive style play, the arbitrarily limited, nerfed, and buffed unit cards make for rather stale single player. It makes me wish that they had taken a play from Men of War's book and offered a lot of options to make it good for either single player types or multiplayer types. That way everyone could have been happy and nobody (single player focused folks like myself) would get left out in the cold.

  If you are a PvP multiplayer focused gamer, this is going to be a good purchase but if you are looking for solid single player content, you should perhaps move on to other titles in the series or other RTS's entirely. To be blunt, Eugen might as well have not even bothered with single player considering how obviously ignored it was.

I can't believe of all the games on my Steam library that I haven't written a review on this one. In a nutshell it's, by far, the best Wargame title to date. But what's there to like/dislike:

The good:

- Replayability from a multiplayer experience. Though the maps remain the same, the way MP games play varies each and every time. Sometimes it's a cake walk. Sometimes it's a good fight. Sometimes it's a kick in the teeth contest. Playing with people you know (even if you don't agree with their personal views on a regular basis) is a satisfying experience. 

- Pace. Again this varies from match to match but it's not a "who-can-click-the-fastest" game. The game rewards a player who can view the situation at hand and respond correctly to it. Thinking two steps ahead can be difficult at times and if anything it's this constant "what next" mentality that rewards a smart player. By far situational awareness is one of the most challenging aspects that I still struggle with each and every time I play. Tip: Play as zoomed out as far as your eyes can handle it. 

- Unit selections. The number is staggering of the number of units you can get your hands on in this game. From Cold War era to more modern entries, chances are your infantry/tank/etc is in this one. 

- Deck builder. One of the best features of the game is making a deck from scratch and then seeing what works/what doesn't work/etc. Because there are SO many units to choose from it isn't easy as it sounds. 

- Best played with friends. Months ago I would have said some type of voice communication was essential to play. Now it's an extra bonus. It's easy to meet people who do enjoy playing and despite the community (that part coming) it's rewarding to help people who are new to the game and made the same mistakes that either I still make (lack of recon/AA/etc) or did make in the past. 

The bad:

- Toxic community doesn't do the word "toxic" justice. For someone new to the game the best advice I can give you is immediately mute Wargame chat (the in-game "twitter" feed is about the best way to put it). If you like to associate with racists, bigots, and people who apparently have nothing better to do than spread hate then maybe that appeals to you. For me I muted this a long time ago. Absolutely no good can come from trying to start a legitimate conversation in wargame chat. And for the toxic players you will meet in a game. Click the mute button. You have been warned...

- Learning curve. The game itself (from a single player perspective) doesn't do a good job of teaching what should be fundamental basics. Using recon effectively is such a key to a good multiplayer experience that you can almost tell a person is new just by looking at their recon percentage. It's a bit late for a proper review but why not.

[h1] Overview	 [/h1]

If you know the series, Red Dragon doesn't really change much. Take ALB and add a few more countries and more units. A few more maps. A dubious artillery buff, to say the least. And there you go.

If you don't know the series, well... Get it now. Especially if you are even remotely interested in military or real time strategy.

[h1] Specifics	 [/h1]

The main thing that Red Dragon purports to innovate from the previous series iterations is [b]naval combat[/b]. It's a great idea on paper but of difficult execution, and unfortunately Eugen didn't pull it off. The ideas of amphibious invasions, maritme support, and even straight out naval battle are all exciting. But somehow it doesn't deliver. The scale is wrong, the balance is off, the tactics are not right, and the naval gameplay is down right terrible. You won't even find multiplayer games for naval battles. On the positive side, it is a somewhat cool novelty for the single player campaign -- with the caveat that if you are focusing on the campaign you are missing out in what makes this game great: Multiplayer. 

The one cool innovation though is [b]amphibious units[/b] [i]in a small scale[/i]. You're able to cross rivers with APCs and such. That's applicable to many maps and it does change the gameplay, giving access to more areas of the map and changing the dynamics around bridges and water. Unfortunately, don't expect to run water-dedicated units.

The [b]maps[/b] are improved. There are a few new ones of course, and in general they are more varied. They have a more rugged terrain which is better than ALBs and much better than EE's flatlands, Where there are larger hills in RD they are more accessible, especially for infantry. The down side of it is that [b]the number of maps is rather small[/b]. If you play quite a bit you'll quite soon find yourself thinking "oh no, not this map again". It's a shame, really, as a large number of maps could add so much to replayability. If Eugen can't deliver it I can't help but think how much this game would benefit from the Steam workshop for player-made maps, or anything of the sort. Unfortunately I don't think it'll ever happen.

The [b]community[/b] has its problems too, especially if you are looking for pickup games. Pub-stomping is widespread, and a huge problem of playing with randoms is the rage-quitting. It happens more in bigger matches (and especially with 10v10) but it does happen in smaller ones too. Your team mate starts out with 2 expensive jets, flies them into enemy territory and gets them all shot down, and since he lost so many points he immediately quits 30 seconds into the match leaving the team seriously jeopardized. That's the norm rather than an exception, quite unfortunately.

The solution for that is the same as for many games: Try to play with people you trust. It's not hard to find people online to play with, so do it. 

Lastly in terms of gameplay is the [b]artillery buff[/b]. I have to say I hate it. Arty in ALB worked just fine but apparently too many people complained it was not lethal enough. No, let me rephrase it: People who didn't know how to use artillery said it was useless. Unfortunately Eugene listened and now arty is a sniping machine that can pin-point kill units across the map.

To start with that irks me because it's [b]unrealistic as shit[/b]. Yeah, I know. Wargame is not meant to be realistic anyway. But it's nice if it has at least some resemblance. The purpose of artillery in the battlefield is not to shred whole armies to pieces with every salvo. Its uses are to affect morale, to wear out and injure, and to majorly suppress whole areas of effect. Shelling is quite the annoyance but it doesn't cause major casualties to dug in units, not even to infantry. But in Red Dragon, one salvo will destroy numerous units and you'll snipe even armoured vehicles with surprising ease.

Its effects on [b]gameplay[/b] are double-sided. On the one hand this buff could be a good thing to deny the opportunity to do trench warfare. You have to be on the move frequently for if you stop an arty salvo will come and destroy a lot of what you have. Giving you incentives to move is not a bad thing. Bad players will invest too much on arty (since it's so powered) so you can just steamrole their defenses and keep moving. The bad thing is that some matches risk turning into a [strike]shit[/strike] shell flinging contest between the two sides and that's as dull as it goes. Shame.

As for the rest, [b]graphics[/b] are absolutely fantastic although you won't be seeing their best part most of the time since you'll be zoomed out to better control your troops. But it's cool to, every once in a while, zoom in close to the battle and see your troops on the ground. Plus it's a great feature for the replays. The [b]controls[/b] are simple and effective, if only a bit demanding on the side of micro-management of some units. I'd prefer some options other RTS titles have such as "skirmish" with which your troops will keep a safe distance from the enemy by themselves. In Wargame you have to tell your troops [i]everything[/i] and they'll act as lemmings. The [b]sounds[/b] are there: Not great but they do their job, although if you are a sound freak you'll likely find them lacking.

One very last thing is that the tutorials and whatnot are ridiculously lacking. Red Dragon is not friendly to new players. But since European Escalation and Airland Battle go on sales often, some times for as little of £1, it might be useful to pick one of those up for doing the tutorials alone.

[h1] Conclusion	 [/h1]

There are to reasons why you shouldn't pick this game up: If you have played EE or ALB and haven't liked it (because RD is more of the same, with small tweaks), or if you are certain the genre doesn't interest you. Anything else and this is a must-have, especially if you can get to play with friends. Just try to do the great tutorials available in the previous titles and/or watch some youtube videos with the basic dos and don'ts.

The learning curve is a little on the steep side, and there is definitely room for improvement on the interface front (selecting units, looking at the status of things, etc) but these are all aspects that you get used to with time. This is because they can't see the enemy, because they're not using their Recon units appropriately. Playing recon takes a little getting used to, but once you have it down, it opens up the rest of the game.

Review:
Really underrated and amazing game and the only real strategy game out there these days besides Starcraft and CMO/CMANO (which I don't even consider a "game"). This game may be frustrating at first but so worth it once you get to know the controls and common units.

Graphics are good. It's just downright fun to fly around your favorite fighter jets (avoid jets while learning the game though) and drive around your favorite tanks. Don't have a favorite tank? Well there are over a hundred to choose from, and you'll find some you like after playing with them. Don't be intimidated by the number of units - you will get used to it and learn them over time. The variety makes the game fun.

Gameplay is good - the controls are fairly easy to grasp (unlike CMO/CMANO) and the game does not demand as much APM (actions per minute: how fast do you need to click) as Starcraft. The "difficulty" is not the controls, it's mostly learning strategies (how/when to use which controls/units) and unit counters. These take a little while to learn. Do not get this game if you only expect to play for 20 hours.

The best part about Wargame is its replayability. There are so many units to choose from, and so many different ways to play, that games don't feel repetitive, like Starcraft, where people have carefully planned builds and timings etc. Hate jets? You don't have to use them at all. Don't want to micromanage artillery? Don't deploy any. I love the flexibilty and general lack of you-lose-if-you-don't-do-X kind of gameplay. Except recon. You lose if you don't use recon units. Use recon units.

As with any game, Wargame has its share of "wow you suck noob why did you do X thing". IGNORE THEM - the other 95% of us are just happy more new people are getting the game! It's better for everyone when new people join, and we'd be happy to have you. Watch out for pubstomping lobbies (i.e. lobbies called "noobs welcome" with 4 very high level players on the other team), but you should be able to find good games/lobbies if you're a little bit patient.

Summary:
I highly recommend Wargame: Red Dragon. It truly is a one-of-a-kind game. If you like strategy or modern/cold war military stuff, or miss Command and Conquer, and are willing to endure a longer-than-usual learning time, you will like Wargame once you get the hang of it. It is extremely replayable and lends itself to a wide variety of playstyles. I wouldn't even call myself "hardcore", but 600 hours later, I'm still here. Come join the fun!

(and seriously, if you get the game, there are players who want to help you learn. the wargame subreddit is a good starting place)

P.S. if you're thinking "I'll wait for the next one", the developers have said they won't make a next one. The hard core fans will not leave this game until the sun explodes. So don't worry about the game dying out, despite the relatively small number of players. We are here to stay, and I rarely have trouble finding games/lobbies/players.

So as of writing I've played this game almost 1200H, so I know what I'm talking about. 

Learning curve:
There is a significant learning curve and it will take a bit of time to get good at this game. First you might think that buying lots of tanks and spamming them in a frontal attack onto the enemy is a good idea, later realizing you didn't account for the enemy having larger firing range on their tank's guns. Also since they where defending they probably also where hidden in the terrain or otherwise taking advantage of it. This is something you will learn, by doing these tactical mistakes. Hell I've made lots of them. Learning the reasons why you made the mistakes can usually be found out fairly intuitively or easily. For example, you can take note of the tank model your enemy used when you charged at him/her, then look up the specs of that tank compared to yours.

Play style & Team play:
There are many ways to win a match. Usually you have an limited amount of currency to buy stuff with and you have to go strong on Anti-Air capability, but weaker on Infantry support or similar. If your opponent then goes with Armored offensive capability and you gambled he would not do so, then you  might lose the game because you can't negate his strengths or exploit his weakness. This becomes much more complicated in big 10vs10 matches, where teamwork will be absolute key, instead of points of a individual player. All this, allows you to develop play styles that fits you and your strategic & tactical thinking best. I like to play with motorized decks, since they provide usually enough of everything, while providing benefits in areas where I'm good at and allows me the most flexibility when adapting to changes in the battle situation.

One important factor in team play is marking the zones that you are going to be responsible for, so you signal to your teammates that they should go somewhere else. This way you avoid critical game starting mistakes, like leaving a zone or flank open, from where the enemy can pour in and attack you in the back. There are still MANY experienced players that haven't understood this fact, a good team  however can cope with this fast and neutralize the threat, but 90+% of the times this is not the case.

My god, where to begin with this near-masterpiece of a game? Be forewarned: this is a REVIEW, not some pathetic little story, profoundly lame joke or cooking recipe. If you want something stupid to read, look anywhere else.

I guess I’ll start with the obvious thing: gameplay. This game is very complex, and I’d only recommend it to an RTS pro who has several RTS games under his or her belt. If you’ve played a game called “R.U.S.E” (which has since been taken off of Steam for reasons unknown), then this game will be very similar to that (not surprising given that the game was made by the same developers, Eugen Systems) one. However, if you’ve played numerous RTS games but haven’t played R.U.S.E, R.U.S.E isn’t mandatory to be able to play – it just makes things a bit easier to learn.

What’s totally insane is the extreme level of detail and diversity when it comes to units. Where R.U.S.E had 7 nations; Wargame: Red Dragon has 21 nations (split between NATO and the Warsaw Pact) with a collective total of over a thousand units. Just like R.U.S.E, each nation has its strengths and weaknesses, but unlike R.U.S.E, you can actually mix and match units from the same faction into a “deck” (to be clear, you cannot have Soviet and NATO troops in the same deck, but you can have, say, British, Canadian and South Korean units in the same NATO deck, or Polish, North Korean and Chinese units in a Warsaw Pact deck); a deck is your deployment group of what units you can call in. There’s lots of units in the game and some of them may look incredibly similar (in rare, rare cases, some are just reskins of other nations’ units) but there are statistical differences that affect your units’ performances, so I recommend looking up guides and videos on what nations’ strengths are. I’m not going to get into depth about that.

Graphically, and as far as detail goes, this game is INCREDIBLE to look at, even when you zoom in real close. The details on just about everything are absolutely marvelous, from water effects to miniature explosions when a tank gets blown to pieces.

Difficulty-wise, this game actually has a unicorn-rare feature that I haven’t seen properly exercised in almost any other RTS game: you can actually choose how the AI, both AI teammates and AI enemies, play the game, because you can set what decks the AI uses. If you want to play like a wimp and give them really crappy units while you roll out the best tanks in the game, be my guest. If the AI’s abusing artillery, you can make a deck that omits artillery so they won’t be able to deploy any. If you want to have an infantry-only war but you have no friends to do it with (this isn’t a guide on how to make friends, so don’t even ask), you can just create a deck with only infantry units in it, assign it to an AI, and you’ll be good to go.

The only issue that makes me call this a “near-masterpiece” was some lag when playing with three friends against four AI, which resulted in one of my friends being dropped from the game. Occasionally it’ll also lag without warning; the battlefield will freeze but after 5-15 seconds it’ll start again.

I wholly recommend this game, primarily for anybody who has a lot of experience with strategy games and enjoys the kind with no unit cap, or maybe you liked R.U.S.E but wanted to try a more advanced version of it or maybe a spiritual sequel to it.

AI spawn rates appears higher than player spawn rates.

Weapons on, or weapons off. No stealth option (return fire when fired upon), no ambush option. No return fire or tactical withdrawal if units are fired upon when a unit is instructed to move from A to B. The unit will continue forward without returning fire and usually be exterminated.

Helicopter dismounts, from "elite" units can take an age.  No tactical flying by helicopters (low flying), though you can adjust the height of the hover), when instructing a helicopter to land while in flight the helicopter will climb ridiculously and expose its position to opposing forces.

Player recce/stealth units are quickly discovered. When directing artillery on to AI units, AI units then move. 

AI never uses helicopter logistics units.

Aircraft fly over enemy controlled territory (where enemy anti-aircraft units are undoubtedly placed) and get shot down quickly, rather than avoid enemy controlled territory. This occurs even when trying to set waypoints (click by click by click by click) to try and manage the approach to a target. 

Player often loses other units while trying to micro manage one unit. 

There is a glitch that remains unfixed (and never will be), when players select units, other units - anywhere on the playing map - will also be selected, and the player usually won't know until random player units move to random areas on the map, often getting attacked and destroyed as the units go for a wander through enemy areas.

And that claxon!!! No option to change the sound, reduce volume or switch off.

Wargame: Red Dragon could be absolutely awesome. 

But it isn't, sadly.

Four out of ten.

Okay. After 500+ hours of wargaming i've decide to write my opinion. Bear in mind Wargame Red Dragon isn't like classic RTS games we've known so far. It is more like Blitzkrieg style but with more immersion, freedom of pace, and visuals. 

Here are my in-depth gameplay review.

There is no Fog Of War. Use recon.
Planning your assault requires planning especially when recon unit is vulnerable to everything else. However, you your troops cannot survive an assault and ambush without recon. You use recon to detect hidden tanks, incoming aircraft, or to find enemy's artilerry. There are several type of recon. Each type has it's purpose realistically.

Tanks rolling enemy infantry in forest? No and don't do it.
Just like real modern battle scenario, tanks usually used in open field. Never ever a commander stupid enough to send tank into forest and urban areas thinking their tanks is some sort of god. Except the terrifying veteran superheavy when it wasn't flanked. Still can be killed. Use your ATGM plane.

Air support. No longer save from ground unit.
Unlike any other classic RTS. Wargame Red Dragon offered a lot of killing opportunity when using airstrike on your target. And unlike any other classic RTS also, aircraft and helo isn't a magic which keep spawning after every cooldown. A helicopter however are useful only in certain situation. You can helorush the infantry and tanks but not a bunch of anti-air support. Also, a single helo shouldn't do a flyby over a forest and urban in happy manners. 

Naval.
To me and several other players. Naval is actually a mistake made by Eugen. There aren't alot of tactical option in naval battle. Which make Total War series naval battle superior. Naval unit's pathing are also the most terrible i've seen.

Artillery and infantry.
These two units always have close relationship even in RTS like Company Of Heroes. Which is why you shouldn't exposed your infantry in the open field and to enemy recon. Or else they'll get raped. However, artillery smoke is my choice when commencing an assault to urban areas using infantry.

Multiplayer.
Here is a few tips. If you looking for large scale unfair batlle, try a server with 50000 points destruction and high income. If you are looking a realistic tactical gameplay, then a server with [Tact] title is for you. I've felt  overpopulated maps are less in entertaining and unproductive compared to low income and scarce in point maps. Be aware that some of player like to leave their keyboard after deployment. 
But in online multiplayer, whether in game or not, community are very cheerful and revolutionary. Warchat sometimes defeat the purpose of the game.

Pros
-Realistic rock-paper-scissor battle system compared to any other RTS.
-Excellent graphic and framerate.
-Lot of unit choices suited for several playstyles.
-Immersive sound.
-Decent background musics.
-Joyful (and hateful) online community.

Cons
-Naval battles are the terrible one.
-Too powerful artilery.
-Uninteresting single player campaign.
-AI were using mongols running towards player.
-Naval units are too powerful to be taken down by anti-naval ground missiles.
-No electronic warfare. Which make modern battles felt less creative.

Edit: I've tried picking it up again, but the micro is just on another level and there's no noob friendly in this game. I tried playing tactical games so there's less units to manage, but again you're probably facing off with someone who has 2000+ games that knows every unit weakness and map strategy by heart. There's not even enough population to consistently get into online games within 10 minutes or so.

I really wanted to like this game but I can't give a recommendation for it. It's designed for online play, but there is only a tiny online community for it. Most public battles are 4 friends on one side vs a bunch of randoms on the other and that goes about as well as you'd think it would.

So what about offline play? The AI is horrendus. All it knows how to do is throw units into a meat grinder. Additionally, sometimes it just stops making moves or spawning units and just sits there (probably a bug, but c'mon this game has been out for what, 2 years now?)

Finally there's the steep learning curve. I like complex games, but forget 1 type of unit and your whole force is destroyed in seconds. The micromanagement is also pretty horrific. Every unit has to be given very specific commands and it will not take any automated action what so ever. Helicopters taking ground fire? They just sit there until they're destroyed. Same goes for tanks. The notification system is terrible. All you hear is "trouble...trouble....trouble..." and no indication of who's in trouble or where they are...yeah lemme just scan the map for the 5 guys standing next to a burning tree...again taking no action on their own to move 3 steps to the left so they don't burn to death.

First off, I'll be absolutely clear, I love this game. It's very fun and unbelievably deep. It can be deeply rewarding when you pull off a perfectly executed counter attack and turn the tide of the game. HOWEVER, I cannot reccomend this game for one simple reason: The community is downright terrible. It's like if /pol had a violent hate child with the USSR. There is one cardinal sin of Wargame, and god help your soul if you commit it; Never, NEVER, ever be a new player to the game learning the ropes.
